contentBlocks.body:
Props are the inputs of a component, and TypeScript is how you document them. Type them with an interface or type alias and destructure them in the parameter list, with default values for optional props. A default applies when the prop is **missing or undefined**, not when it is `null`.

In React 19, `ref` is an ordinary prop for function components, so you rarely need `forwardRef` anymore. `children` is typed as `React.ReactNode`, which accepts anything renderable: elements, strings, numbers, arrays, null, and booleans.

When one component can render in two shapes, model the props as a **discriminated union**. The shared literal field (here `as`) tells TypeScript which other props are allowed, so invalid combinations fail at compile time instead of at runtime:

- `<Action as="link" href="/products" />` is valid
- `<Action as="link" disabled />` does not compile: links have no `disabled`
- inside the component, `if (props.as === "link")` narrows `props` so `props.href` is available
A `<button>` inside a `<form>` defaults to `type="submit"`. A reusable Button component should default to `type="button"` so an Edit or Cancel button does not submit the form by accident.

knowledgeItems.prompt: With function Card({ size = "md" }: Props), what is size when rendered as <Card size={null} />?

payload.explanation: Destructuring defaults, like default parameters, only apply to undefined. An explicit null is passed through (and TypeScript would reject it unless the type allows null).

knowledgeItems.prompt: What is the best type for a prop that can hold any renderable content?

payload.explanation: ReactNode covers elements, strings, numbers, arrays, null and booleans. JSX.Element only allows a single element.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Complete the rel value that should accompany target="_blank" on external links.
Resolve discriminated-union props for an Action component into the tag, class, text, and attributes it would render, applying defaults.
